headline: Oil to stay volatile in $70–$90/bbl range near-term; not a believer in the 2027 glut narrative pushing prices to the $60s
reasoning: Mukesh Sahdev sees oil remaining volatile in a broad $70–$90 per barrel range through year-end, with a narrower trading band of $75–$85 as the base case. He dismisses the widely discussed 2027 oil glut scenario, saying there is 'a lot more to happen' before that materialises. A key swing factor is whether a US–China meeting between Xi Jinping and the US president occurs, as China is simultaneously losing Venezuelan, Iranian and Russian barrels due to sanctions and the Ukraine conflict. He also notes that US refining demand may not slow down as seasonally expected, which could provide ongoing crude consumption support. All of these supply disruptions converge on China, making geopolitical diplomacy the critical variable for oil market resolution.
quote: My view is that the oil price will stay volatile in this broad 70 to $90 per barrel range. And if you want a narrow range, I think 75 to $85 is probably the range. Yes. A lot of, uh, in 2027, a lot of people are talking about the oil glut being back, and the oil prices will go down to the 60s and 70s. I'm not a believer, uh, in that glut story as yet. I think there's a lot more to happen before that. But for the short term, till end of the year, I think, uh, you know, this sort of, uh, uh, in the range of 70 to 90 and 75 to 85 is the right, uh, playing point.
episode_title: Why oil’s headline rally may have more bark than bite

headline: All roads lead to China: a Xi-Trump meeting is a necessary condition for resolving the oil market dislocation
reasoning: Sahdev argues that the US strategy of gaining leverage via Venezuela, Iran, and Russia is ultimately aimed at China, which is the primary buyer losing barrels from all three sources simultaneously. He sees Venezuela as a US success story, with potential to ramp production back toward historical highs of 3.5 mbpd. But without a high-level US-China political resolution — specifically a meeting between Xi Jinping and the US president — there is no structural solver for global oil market imbalances, as China remains the central demand node for all three sanctioned supply streams.
quote: Whether it's Venezuela, whether it's Iran or Russia, I think all roads lead to China. And that's why the meeting which might happen between, uh, XI Jinping and the US president is very critical. Uh, without that, I don't think there is a solver for the oil markets.
episode_title: Why oil’s headline rally may have more bark than bite

headline: Global crude flow reshuffle underway as Venezuela barrels shift from China to US Gulf Coast and India, creating a quality-of-crude mismatch
reasoning: Sahdev explains that Venezuelan heavy crude historically required light naphtha inputs from Russia, China, and Iran, with output flowing to China. Now the US has cut that arrangement, supplying its own naphtha to Venezuela and directing output toward the US Gulf Coast. However, US Gulf refineries have a limit on heavy barrel intake, so India — with complex refineries like Reliance and Indian Oil capable of processing heavy, sour Venezuelan crude — becomes a beneficiary. China has effectively lost Venezuelan, Iranian, and some Russian barrels simultaneously, creating a multilayered reshuffle of crude, naphtha, and fuel oil flows he calls 'chem politics.'
quote: India in that case is a bit of a lucky advantage because India has very complex refineries like Reliance and Indian Oil, which can process the dirty, heavy, sort of toxic, I would say Venezuelan kind of crudes at an advantage price. So there is a lot of reshuffle, not just of the crude but naphtha, but fuel oil. It's, I would say not just geopolitics, I would call it. It is chem politics at play.
episode_title: Why oil’s headline rally may have more bark than bite

headline: Headline geopolitical risk overstated; dark trade, storage, and Venezuela supply check prices with $95 as likely top-end
reasoning: Sahdev argues that while oil prices are rising on headlines around US strikes on Iran and Strait of Hormuz tensions, the underlying fundamentals are less bullish than the market reaction implies. A large volume of crude is moving via 'dark trade' — with transponders turned off — meaning supply leakages are not captured in tracking data, and this hidden supply is keeping actual delivered volumes higher than official numbers suggest. US peak summer demand is over, Venezuela has ramped production toward 1.2 million barrels per day (once near 3.5 mbpd), and some Russian diesel and Caspian flows continue. He also notes voyage time uncertainty (not a supply shortage) is what keeps prices elevated, and pegs $95/bbl as roughly the top end of the range.
quote: I believe Venezuela is a noose around there. Dark trade is the news that's keeping the oil price is probably. And my guess is 95 is probably the top end... I think the attacks that were happening on Kazakhstan and some of the Caspian barrels, uh, were also have some of somehow slowed down. So, yes, I would say dark trades, uh, to some extent. Also the US, uh, summer season is over. The peak summer season is likely over now, and that probably keeps a check on the oil price.
episode_title: Why oil’s headline rally may have more bark than bite

headline: Oil price forecast range of $70-$90 per barrel with upside risk if Middle East conflict remains unresolved
reasoning: Sahdev believes the scene is being set for higher oil prices given the combination of the Hormuz closure and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, but maintains a base range of $70-90 per barrel as his volatile range, with prices occasionally crossing above that level. He notes that if there is no diplomatic resolution in the Middle East, the market could test recent highs seen a couple of months ago.
quote: The scene is probably getting set up for higher oil prices, but I would say that probably my range is between 70 to 90. Volatile range, uh, is what I would put uh, for occasional times it crosses.
episode_title: Why oil troubles could continue spilling

headline: Russia's 7–8 mb/d export system poses a larger structural oil supply risk than a Strait of Hormuz closure
reasoning: Mukesh Sahdev argues that Russia's oil export system, running at 7–8 million barrels per day, represents a more significant tail risk to global oil supply than a Hormuz disruption. He notes that Russia is also leaking heavier crude feedstocks to markets, which serve as a substitute for crude oil. A deterioration or 'tailspin' in Russia's oil system could be a much bigger problem for global markets than Hormuz. He frames the current situation as 'Hormuz 2.0' with underlying structural challenges that are difficult to resolve quickly.
quote: Russia has an oil system, 7 to 8 million barrels of exports. If it goes into a bit of a tailspin, that is a much bigger problem than Hormuz. The scene is probably getting set up for higher oil prices... I think the underlying structural challenge is much bigger in this Hormuz 2.0. So I don't see easy way out.
episode_title: Why oil troubles could continue spilling

headline: Hormuz 2.0 closure likely to create sharper supply shock for Asian oil markets than the first crisis, with physical shortfalls expected within 2-3 weeks
reasoning: Mukesh Sahdev argues that the current Hormuz closure (Hormuz 2.0) could be worse for Asian economies than the first crisis because Gulf producers had already reversed course to route barrels via Hormuz again, meaning ships are now loaded and oil needs to be pumped back into alternative pipelines and routes, which is logistically difficult. Asian buyers typically secure crude two months in advance and had moved vessels toward the Gulf expecting it to reopen, so they may not reach Atlantic barrels in time. US crude, gasoline and diesel stocks are already very low, adding another pressure point. Sahdev disagrees with the 10-week timeline for physical shortfalls cited by CBA's Vivek Dhar, saying the impact could be felt in a much shorter timeframe, with the next 2-3 weeks described as 'very, very critical'. Current pricing reflects some geopolitical risk premium but not the full premium warranted by the risks.
quote: No. At this point of time. Uh, you know, this week, next week, uh, the market is seeing some data where the crude arrivals in Asia is looking good because the barrels are already on the sea. The insurance policy is on the sea. But the only question is it will not last much longer than two, two weeks or three weeks time... So I think ten weeks these days in oil markets is probably a long time to talk. I would rather focus that the next 2 or 3 weeks are very, very critical.
episode_title: Why oil troubles could continue spilling

headline: Ukraine strikes on Russian oil infrastructure represent a major black swan risk for global oil supply, potentially more disruptive than the Hormuz closure alone
reasoning: Sahdev notes Ukraine is now striking 3,000km deep into Russia, targeting refineries that supply domestic products, which forces Russia to export raw crude rather than refined products. To export, Russia needs US sanctions waivers, which come at a high cost. Russian barrels are being routed toward Asia via the Red Sea, but with Hormuz also disrupted, Saudi Arabia is maxing out its East-West pipeline and Red Sea capacity at 5 million gallons. The Ukraine crisis is causing crude congestion, reducing availability of diesel, jet fuel and gas that Russia was exporting, and also cutting off heavier feedstocks/crude substitutes that Russia was leaking to markets. Sahdev estimates Russia's 7-8 million barrels per day of exports going into 'a bit of a tailspin' would be a bigger problem than the Hormuz closure on its own.
quote: I think that's the one big black swan event which the markets need to be prepared with. Even if we put lower probability. For now, what is really happening is Ukraine is striking now 3000km into deep into Russia. It is striking the refineries which provide not the export products, but the domestic uh products which cause political problems and challenge for the Russian government... in some ways, I think Russia has an oil system, 7 to 8 million barrels of exports. If it goes into a bit of a tailspin, that is a much bigger problem than Hormuz.
episode_title: Why oil troubles could continue spilling
